impacts.caseName: Teva Pharmaceuticals International GmbH v. Eli Lilly and Company
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court erred in granting judgment as a matter of law that patent claims directed to methods of treating headache using humanized anti-CGRP antagonist antibodies were invalid for failure to satisfy the written-description and enablement requirements of 35 U.S.C. § 112.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's JMOL of invalidity of Teva's headache patents covering methods of using humanized anti-CGRP antagonist antibodies to treat headache, and remanded. This case involves Teva's Ajovy product and Lilly's competing CGRP-pathway migraine treatment, with significant implications for the scope of patent protection available for biologic drug classes.
impacts.positiveImplications: Strengthens patent protection for biologic innovators by affirming that genus claims to antibody methods-of-treatment can satisfy written description and enablement requirements even when only one specific antibody is disclosed, provided the specification adequately teaches how to make and use the claimed class.
impacts.negativeImplications: Biosimilar and competing biologic developers face increased risk that broad method-of-treatment claims covering antibody classes will survive validity challenges, potentially limiting market entry for competing biologics.

impacts.caseName: Trustees of Columbia University v. Gen Digital Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patent claims directed to methods for detecting anomalous program executions by emulating a program and comparing function calls to a model are directed to an abstract idea under step one of the Alice framework, and whether the district court erred in denying JMOL on damages for foreign sales.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the judgment, holding that Columbia's cybersecurity patents claiming methods of detecting anomalous program executions are abstract at Alice step one, requiring remand for step two analysis. The court also held that damages based on Norton's foreign sales were improperly awarded, limiting extraterritorial reach of U.S. patent damages. The jury had awarded $185 million in damages.
impacts.positiveImplications: Technology companies benefit from the court's rigorous application of Alice step one to cybersecurity method claims and from the limitation on damages based on foreign sales, reducing exposure in patent infringement suits involving global software distribution.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders in cybersecurity and software face heightened eligibility risk, as the court found that emulation-based anomaly detection methods are abstract. Universities and research institutions relying on software patents may see reduced damages and increased invalidity challenges.

impacts.caseName: International Medical Devices, Inc. v. Cornell
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the jury's finding that asserted trade secrets were protectable under California law was supported by a legally sufficient evidentiary basis, and whether ideas that are generally known can constitute an inventive contribution for patent inventorship purposes.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the denial of JMOL on trade secret misappropriation claims, holding that the plaintiff failed to provide legally sufficient evidence that the asserted trade secrets were protectable because the underlying ideas were generally known. The court also reversed the patent inventorship determination on the same basis. The counterfeiting claim and associated damages were affirmed.
impacts.positiveImplications: Companies defending against trade secret claims benefit from the court's requirement that plaintiffs must demonstrate with sufficient evidence that asserted trade secrets are not generally known in the industry, raising the evidentiary bar for trade secret plaintiffs.
impacts.negativeImplications: Trade secret holders face a higher burden of proof to establish that their claimed secrets are not generally known, potentially undermining enforcement of trade secret protections in industries where foundational concepts are widely shared.

impacts.caseName: VLSI Technology LLC v. Intel Corporation
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court erred in granting summary judgment of noninfringement of a multicore processor patent based on extraterritoriality and rejection of the doctrine of equivalents theory, and whether the court properly struck certain damages expert theories.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed in part the grant of summary judgment of noninfringement of VLSI's multicore processor patent against Intel, finding genuine disputes of material fact on the extraterritoriality ground. The court affirmed on the doctrine of equivalents ground but reversed the exclusion of certain damages expert theories. The case was remanded for further proceedings.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders asserting claims against semiconductor and processor manufacturers benefit from the court's analysis permitting infringement claims where substantial steps of the patented method occur domestically, even if some components are manufactured or designed abroad.
impacts.negativeImplications: Semiconductor companies face expanded infringement exposure for multicore processor patents where design or testing occurs in the U.S., even if final manufacturing occurs overseas.

impacts.caseName: Global Tubing LLC v. Tenaris Coiled Tubes LLC
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether genuine disputes of material fact precluded summary judgment on inequitable conduct in patent prosecution and on a Walker Process antitrust fraud claim for attempted monopolization.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated summary judgment on both inequitable conduct (granted in favor of Global Tubing) and Walker Process fraud (granted in favor of Tenaris), finding genuine disputes of material fact on both issues. The case involves Tenaris's acquisition of prior art (CYMAX technology) and its failure to disclose that art during patent prosecution for its competing coiled tubing product.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent challengers benefit from the court's willingness to find triable issues on inequitable conduct when a patent applicant acquires prior art through corporate acquisition and arguably conceals it during prosecution. This strengthens defenses against patents procured through potential fraud.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders who acquire businesses with prior art face heightened litigation risk if they fail to disclose that acquired prior art during patent prosecution, as courts may find sufficient evidence of intent to deceive to survive summary judgment.

impacts.caseName: Constellation Designs, LLC v. LG Electronics Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patent claims directed to non-uniform constellations for digital communication systems are patent-eligible under 35 U.S.C. § 101, and whether the district court properly denied JMOL of non-infringement and no damages.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated summary judgment of patent eligibility for certain claims of two patents directed to non-uniform constellation designs for digital communications, while affirming eligibility for claims of two other patents that recited specific technical implementations. The court affirmed the denial of JMOL on infringement and damages. This case provides important guidance on the Alice eligibility framework for communications technology patents.
impacts.positiveImplications: Technology companies accused of infringement benefit from the court's vacatur of eligibility for broadly-claimed mathematical optimization patents, reinforcing that claims to mathematical relationships without sufficient technical implementation may be ineligible.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders in communications technology face split outcomes on eligibility depending on claim specificity; broadly-drafted claims reciting optimized mathematical relationships risk invalidation while more technically detailed claims may survive.

impacts.caseName: Actelion Pharmaceuticals Ltd v. Mylan Pharmaceuticals Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the claim term 'a pH of 13 or higher' in pharmaceutical composition patents refers to pH measured at a standard temperature in the field, and whether the patentee was barred from asserting infringement under the doctrine of equivalents.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the finding of no literal infringement of Actelion's epoprostenol formulation patents, agreeing that the claim term 'pH of 13 or higher' refers to pH measured at a standard temperature (25°C). The court also affirmed that Actelion was barred from asserting and had not proved infringement by equivalents. This ruling impacts ANDA litigation for generic versions of Actelion's Veletri hypertension drug.
impacts.positiveImplications: Generic pharmaceutical companies benefit from claim construction requiring pH measurements at field-standard temperatures, enabling them to design around formulation patents by demonstrating non-infringement under standard measurement conditions.
impacts.negativeImplications: Branded pharmaceutical companies face narrower claim scope for formulation patents where measurement conditions are not explicitly specified, potentially easing generic market entry for temperature-sensitive pharmaceutical compositions.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a Rule 30(b)(6) corporate representative may testify outside personal knowledge at summary judgment, and whether the on-sale bar of 35 U.S.C. § 102(b) requires that a prior art sale expressly disclose the device's claimed functionality.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed summary judgment of invalidity under the on-sale bar, holding that Rule 30(b)(6) corporate representatives may testify beyond personal knowledge and that the on-sale bar does not require that the prior art sale expressly disclose the device's functionality. The court also held that source code is not hearsay because it constitutes computer commands rather than statements.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers benefit from the ruling that 30(b)(6) testimony may be used at summary judgment even when the witness lacks personal knowledge, and that prior commercial sales invalidate patents without requiring express disclosure of the sold product's internal functionality.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders face broader on-sale bar exposure, as competitors can invalidate patents by proving pre-critical-date sales of embodying products without needing to show that buyers or sellers understood or disclosed the claimed technical features.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the ITC properly found that Apple's importation and sale of Apple Watch models with blood oxygen measurement functionality violated Section 337 of the Tariff Act by infringing Masimo's patents covering wearable blood oxygen measurement devices.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the ITC's finding that Apple violated Section 337 and upheld the limited exclusion order barring importation of Apple Watch models incorporating blood oxygen features covered by Masimo's patents. The court found no error in the Commission's domestic industry determination, validity rulings, or infringement findings.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders benefit from the affirmance of ITC exclusion orders against major technology companies, confirming that the ITC remains a powerful venue for enforcing patents against imported products and that wearable health technology patents can support exclusion orders.
impacts.negativeImplications: Major technology companies face significant commercial disruption from ITC exclusion orders that can bar importation of flagship consumer products, creating pressure to design around patented features or negotiate licenses.

impacts.caseName: Ascendis Pharma A/S v. BioMarin Pharmaceutical Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a respondent in an ITC proceeding may obtain a mandatory stay under 28 U.S.C. § 1659(a)(2) of its refiled declaratory judgment action when it had previously filed a declaratory judgment action and missed the deadline for seeking a stay.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit held that an ITC respondent cannot circumvent the statutory deadline for seeking a mandatory stay of a parallel district court action by voluntarily dismissing its original action and refiling a new one. This prevents gamesmanship in the coordination between ITC investigations and parallel district court patent litigation.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders pursuing ITC investigations benefit from the ruling preventing respondents from manipulating stay deadlines through strategic refiling, ensuring that parallel district court proceedings can advance and provide additional remedies.
impacts.negativeImplications: ITC respondents lose the ability to strategically refile declaratory judgment actions to obtain mandatory stays they missed in the original action, reducing their ability to control the timing and sequencing of parallel patent disputes.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court abused its discretion in excluding a damages expert report for using an incorrect royalty base and then granting summary judgment based on the absence of a quantified remedy.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the exclusion of Exafer's damages expert report and vacated summary judgment in favor of Microsoft, holding that the district court applied an overly rigid standard in evaluating the expert's royalty methodology. The court found that disagreements over the appropriate royalty base go to the weight, not the admissibility, of expert testimony.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders benefit from the ruling that disputes over the appropriate royalty base in damages calculations are matters of weight for the jury, not admissibility, making it more difficult for defendants to secure summary judgment by excluding damages evidence.
impacts.negativeImplications: Technology companies defending patent suits face increased difficulty in excluding damages expert testimony at the Daubert stage, potentially resulting in larger damages awards reaching the jury.

impacts.caseName: Federal Express Corporation v. Qualcomm Incorporated
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the Board erred in its obviousness determination of challenged patent claims, particularly regarding the construction of the 'predetermined time delay' limitation, in an IPR petition filed by a non-party to the underlying district court litigation on the statutory deadline of the actual defendant.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the Board's obviousness determination and remanded, finding error in the Board's analysis of the challenged claims. The case also raised significant questions about potential abuse of the IPR system by third parties filing petitions on behalf of or in coordination with time-barred parties, though the court declined to review the Board's denial of FedEx's termination motion.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders benefit from the vacatur of an obviousness finding and the court's scrutiny of potentially coordinated IPR filings by third parties designed to circumvent the one-year time bar, preserving the integrity of patent rights against strategic gaming of the IPR system.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies seeking to challenge patents through IPR face uncertainty when coordinating with time-barred parties, as the court's decision signals potential judicial scrutiny of such arrangements even though the specific challenge was not reviewed on the merits.

impacts.caseName: National Veterans Legal Services Program v. United States
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court properly approved a $125 million class action settlement of claims that the federal judiciary overcharged PACER users, and whether the settlement's attorneys' fees and incentive awards were appropriate.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the approval of a $125 million settlement in a nationwide class action alleging that PACER fees were used to fund expenses beyond the cost of operating the PACER system. The court upheld the attorneys' fees, costs, and incentive awards to the three nonprofit class representatives, finding that the settlement provided full or substantial reimbursement to hundreds of thousands of PACER users.
impacts.positiveImplications: The settlement establishes that excessive government fees can be successfully challenged through class action litigation, and the approval of incentive awards to nonprofit class representatives encourages public interest organizations to serve as class representatives.

impacts.caseName: Willis Electric Co., Ltd. v. Polygroup Ltd. (Macao Commercial Offshore)
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court properly denied Polygroup's motion for JMOL of obviousness and for a new trial on damages regarding a patent for pre-lit artificial trees with integrated mechanical and electrical connections.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the denial of JMOL of obviousness and the denial of a new trial on damages for Willis's patent on pre-lit artificial Christmas trees with coaxial trunk connectors enabling simultaneous mechanical and electrical connections. The ruling upholds substantial damages for consumer product patents where the claimed innovation simplifies product assembly.
impacts.positiveImplications: Consumer product patent holders benefit from the court's affirmance that jury findings on non-obviousness and damages are entitled to deference, supporting enforcement of patents on practical product improvements even where individual elements may exist in the prior art.
impacts.negativeImplications: Competitors in consumer products face continued risk of substantial damages for infringing patents on product assembly innovations, even where the claimed technology involves combinations of known components.
